abstract: Salinity limits alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) productivity, yet integrative physiological markers of cultivar tolerance remain poorly defined. This study aimed to identify candidate physiological indicators of salt tolerance by integrating growth, metabolic, and time-resolved photosynthetic traits across diverse alfalfa cultivars. We exposed nine alfalfa cultivars to a 200 mM NaCl hydroponic shock and monitored their physiological responses over 14 days. We assessed shoot and root growth, leaf Na+/K+ homeostasis, carbohydrate partitioning, dynamic chlorophyll a fluorescence (ChlF), and NIRS-based forage quality. Salinity elicited cultivar-dependent responses. Tolerant cultivars maintained shoot biomass, restricted foliar Na+ accumulation, preserved leaf starch reserves, and progressively recovered Phi2 and linear electron flow (LEF) following initial declines. In contrast, less tolerant cultivars showed persistent growth inhibition, reduced leaf starch, and persistent photochemical impairment. At 7 and 14 dpt, PItotal and Fv'/Fm' correlated positively with final biomass, whereas PhiNPQ and PhiNO showed negative correlations. Notably, the association between regulated energy dissipation (PhiNPQ) and biomass retention inverted over time, shifting from an early photoprotective mechanism at 1 dpt to a sign of chronic photoinhibitory strain by 7 and 14 dpt. These responses were accompanied by cultivar-specific changes in Na+/K+; balance, soluble sugars, starch, and forage quality. Tracking time-resolved PSII photochemistry reveals that maintaining PItotal and Fv'/Fm' under saline stress offers an accurate, non-invasive proxy for evaluating cultivar resilience. Their integration into high-throughput phenotyping and breeding programs could facilitate the selection of resilient cultivars. Field validation should consider both biomass production and forage nutritional quality.
